Plant
plant
v.t. and n. (rendering Hebrew nata', Greek phyteuō)
From Latin planta, a sprout or slip, and plantare, to set in the ground with the sole of the foot. Hebrew nata' means to fix or fasten in, and is used of trees, of vineyards, of tent pegs, and of a people settled in a land God has given them.

Biblical Definition

To plant is to put something where it will draw life from ground it did not choose, and Scripture makes the figure carry the doctrine of election, of nurture, and of judgment. The blessed man of the first Psalm is not self-supporting: he “shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psalm 1:3) — planted, passive, and therefore fruitful in due time. The Lord Jesus applies the same figure to false religion with terrible economy: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Matthew 15:13) — the test is not vigour or reputation but origin. Paul distributes the labour and reserves the outcome: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6) — a sentence that has kept many a minister sane. And Jeremiah is commissioned with the whole vocabulary of demolition and cultivation at once: set “over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:10) — four verbs of tearing down before the two of building, which is the usual order of God's work in a man and in a nation. Planting is God's prerogative; watering is the servant's duty; and increase is never anyone's achievement.

Webster 1828 Definition

To put in the ground and cover, as seed or a slip, for growth; to set, fix, or establish. In Scripture, the man planted by rivers of water, every plant not planted by the Father rooted up, Paul planting and Apollos watering while God gives the increase, and the prophet set to pull down and to plant.

PLANT, v.t. 1. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set, as a shrub or tree.

2. To engender; to set the first inhabitants; to settle; as, to plant a colony.

3. To fix; to establish; as, to plant a church or an institution.

4. From Latin planta, a slip or shoot, and plantare, to set with the foot.

5. In Scripture, like a tree planted by the rivers of water, Ps. 1; I have planted, Apollos watered, 1 Cor. 3.

Key Scripture

Psalm 1:3 — "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper."

Matthew 15:13 — "But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up."

1 Corinthians 3:6 — "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."

Jeremiah 1:10 — "See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant."

Modern Corruption

Increase is credited to the labourer, so that ministerial success becomes a measure of the man; and the test of a religious movement becomes its growth rather than whether the Father planted it.

expand to see more

Matthew 15:13 supplies a criterion the age has almost entirely abandoned. Confronted with a religious system that was flourishing, respected, and hostile to Him, the Lord did not ask whether it was growing; He asked who planted it, and pronounced its end. Modern evaluation reverses the test. A movement that draws crowds, plants campuses, and reports numbers is presumed to have God's blessing on it, and to question it is treated as envy. But Scripture repeatedly shows error growing fast and truth held by a remnant — four hundred prophets of Baal against one Micaiah, a whole nation against Jeremiah, the multitude crying crucify him. Growth proves that something is being planted; it does not prove who planted it. The examination has to be doctrinal, and the fruit that finally tells is the fruit of the Spirit and of sound teaching, not attendance.

The second error attaches the increase to the man. Paul had every ground for taking credit at Corinth — he founded the church, he suffered for it, he loved it — and he refuses the credit in the plainest terms: neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. This is not modesty; it is theology, and it cuts both ways for the labourer. It forbids him to boast when the field flourishes, and it forbids him to despair when it does not, because the increase was never in his hands. The principle to recover is that faithfulness in planting and watering is the whole of a servant's duty, and the harvest is the Lord's business. Where that is believed, ministers stop competing and start working.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nata', to plant or fix in; matta', a plantation or that which is planted; Greek phyteuō, to plant, and phyteia, a planting or plant.

expand to see more

Hebrew nata' (H5193) — to plant, fasten, establish; used of vineyards, of Eden, and of Israel planted in the land.

Hebrew matta' (H4302) — a plantation, or a plant; “the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified” (Isaiah 61:3).

Hebrew shathal (H8362) — to transplant; the verb of Psalm 1:3, a tree deliberately set beside water.

Greek phyteuō (G5452) — to plant; used of Paul's founding labour at Corinth (1 Corinthians 3:6).

Greek phyteia (G5451) — a planting, a plant; “every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted” (Matthew 15:13).

Usage

"Of the fruitful believer's dependence: like a tree planted by the rivers of water (Psalm 1:3)."

"Of the test of a religious system: Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up (Matthew 15:13)."

"Of divided labour and undivided credit: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6)."
